Eggs of the Smooth newt Lissotriton vulgaris, deposited individually and wrapped in aquatic vegetation, undergo embryogenesis at a temperature-dependent pace; when incubated at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the duration from oviposition to eclosion averages approximately 25 days [ab = approximately 25 days]. This incubation period is relatively protracted compared to many pond-breeding urodeles, reflecting the lower metabolic rates characteristic of small-bodied temperate amphibians. Upon hatching, the aquatic larvae are quite diminutive, measuring only 0.84 centimeters [Lb = 0.84 centimeters] in total length and possessing an initial wet weight of just 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams]. This minute body size at the onset of exogenous feeding imposes considerable constraints on foraging efficiency and vulnerability to predation, compelling rapid growth during the early larval phase to escape the size window of highest mortality. The subsequent larval period, during which individuals feed actively on zooplankton and small invertebrates, spans several months under typical thermal regimes. The completion of metamorphosis, marked by gill resorption and the transition to a terrestrial eft stage, represents a critical developmental bottleneck in the life cycle of this species.

Larval development proceeds steadily at a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], with individuals attaining an average total length of 3 centimeters  after approximately 240 days of growth. This length measurement, recorded at the 240-day mark, provides a useful metric for comparing growth trajectories among cohorts raised under controlled thermal conditions or across different natural ponds. Continued somatic expansion over the following months is substantial; by 970 days post-hatching, juveniles raised under the same thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] reach a mean total length of 8.5 centimeters . The growth increment between these two age points highlights a period of rapid linear extension that precedes the approach to asymptotic size. Field surveys indicate that wild populations exhibit considerable variation around these laboratory-derived figures, likely mediated by food availability and intraspecific competition. Nevertheless, these data establish a clear baseline for the species' growth performance at a moderate temperature, comparable to values reported for congeneric species such as Lissotriton helveticus under similar rearing conditions.

Sexual maturation in Lissotriton vulgaris is attained after an extended juvenile phase spent foraging in terrestrial habitats and returning to water bodies only during the breeding season. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the time elapsed since birth at puberty averages approximately 600 days [tp = approximately 600 days]. At this developmental milestone, individuals exhibit a total length at puberty of 5.4 centimeters [Lp = 5.4 centimeters] and a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 0.728 grams [Wwp = 0.728 grams]. The relationship between length and mass at this stage conforms to the expected allometric scaling for the species, with the pubertal weight representing roughly fourteen percent of the ultimate adult mass. The onset of gonadal activity is accompanied by the development of secondary sexual characteristics, including the dorsal crest and pronounced toe fringes in males. The protracted duration of the juvenile period, exceeding one and a half years before reproductive competence is achieved, is a common life-history strategy among small-bodied newts, allowing sufficient time for the accumulation of somatic reserves necessary to support the energetic demands of breeding.

Adults of the Smooth newt achieve their ultimate or asymptotic dimensions after several years of sustained growth, a pattern typical of indeterminate growers. The ultimate total length recorded for this species is 10.4 centimeters [Li = 10.4 centimeters], corresponding to an ultimate wet weight of approximately 5.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 5.2 grams], making the Smooth newt one of the smaller members of the family Salamandridae within its European range. The maximum reproductive rate, calculated from the mean number of eggs deposited per day over the peak breeding season, reaches 0.96 eggs per day [Ri = 0.96 eggs per day] at 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This value translates into a substantial annual fecundity: reproductively active females typically deposit between 200 and 300 eggs over the course of a single breeding season, often partitioned into several distinct clutches. Egg diameter averages approximately 2.5 millimeters, consistent with the calculated birth weight and reflecting the limited per-offspring investment characteristic of species that produce large numbers of pelagic or shallow-water eggs.

The species' lifespan represents the culmination of its slow life-history strategy, with individuals capable of surviving for multiple decades under benign conditions when predation and disease are minimized. Under the constant thermal regime of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for Lissotriton vulgaris, determined from mark-recapture studies and captive maintenance records, reaches approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years], although most wild individuals likely die considerably earlier due to environmental hazards. The metamorphic transition from aquatic larva to terrestrial juvenile occurs at a mean age of 113 days after hatching , calculated from the same thermal background at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This relatively short larval duration, combined with the protracted juvenile and adult phases, defines a life cycle wherein early mortality is high but survivors enjoy a long reproductive window. Comparisons with other European newts, such as Triturus cristatus, reveal that the Smooth newt achieves a somewhat shorter maximum lifespan but compensates through earlier maturation and higher annual fecundity, reflecting divergent adaptive responses to the respective selective pressures of their aquatic and terrestrial environments.
